criteria.description: Correctly identifies the O(n^2) storage / O(n^3) solve cost problem for large n.
Correctly identifies the general strategy: approximate curvature information more cheaply, rather than computing the exact Hessian.

commonErrors: Only mentioning 'it's expensive' without quantifying why (the n^2/n^3 scaling).
Not connecting this back to the covariant-gradient theme from MATH-05 (correcting the gradient with curvature information).

solutions.fullSolution: The exact Hessian has n^2 entries; computing all of them generally costs as much as differentiating the gradient n times, storing it costs O(n^2) memory, and solving a linear system with it (as Newton's method requires) costs O(n^3) in general. For n in the thousands or millions, all three become infeasible. The general strategy in this module: get a useful APPROXIMATION of curvature information cheaply, either by exploiting problem structure (Gauss-Newton, for least-squares problems specifically), building an approximation incrementally from a history of gradient observations (quasi-Newton/BFGS), or avoiding forming the Hessian at all via an iterative method (conjugate gradient). This is the same theme as MATH-05's covariant gradient (correct the plain gradient using curvature), just now focused on how to obtain that curvature information affordably.

criteria.description: Correctly derives grad f(x) = J(x)^T r(x) via the chain rule on the sum-of-squares.
Correctly differentiates once more (product rule) to get H(x) = J^T J + sum_i r_i * (Hessian of r_i).
Correctly explains why the dropped term is small specifically when residuals are small, i.e. near a good fit.

commonErrors: Forgetting the product rule has TWO terms when differentiating J(x)^T r(x) again (one from J^T changing, one from r changing).
Not connecting 'residuals near zero' to 'near convergence', missing why this approximation is most accurate exactly when it matters most.

solutions.fullSolution:
f(x) = (1/2) sum_i r_i(x)^2. partial f/partial x_k = sum_i r_i(x) * partial r_i/partial x_k = sum_i r_i(x) J_ik = [J(x)^T r(x)]_k. So grad f(x) = J(x)^T r(x).

Differentiating grad f(x) = J(x)^T r(x) w.r.t. x again, using the product rule (J^T itself depends on x too): H(x) = J(x)^T J(x) + sum_i r_i(x) * Hessian(r_i)(x), where the second term comes from differentiating J(x)^T (each row/column of which depends on x through the second derivatives of each r_i).

Gauss-Newton drops the second term, sum_i r_i(x) Hessian(r_i)(x), approximating H(x) ~= J(x)^T J(x). This term is weighted by the residuals r_i(x) themselves, so it vanishes as the fit improves (residuals shrink toward 0), regardless of how curved each r_i is. So the approximation is best exactly near a good fit, i.e. near convergence, which is precisely when an accurate Hessian approximation matters most for fast local convergence.

J = [[1,0],[0,1],[1,1]], r(x0) = [-1,-2,-2]. J^T J = [[2,1],[1,2]]. J^T r(x0) = [-3,-4]. delta = -(J^T J)^-1 (J^T r) solves [[2,1],[1,2]] delta = [3,4], giving delta = [0.667, 1.667]. x1 = x0 + delta = [0.667, 1.667]. Second component: 1.667. (Verified with NumPy; since the residual is linear here, this Gauss-Newton step is exact, landing on the true least-squares solution in one step, not merely an approximation.)

criteria.description: Correctly writes out phi_1, phi_2, phi_3 using the boundary values x_0=x_-1=0.
Correctly computes the Jacobian J, all six partial derivatives.
Correctly explains the zero entries as reflecting locality of dependence (banded structure).

commonErrors: Forgetting to substitute the given boundary values x_0=x_-1=0 into phi_1, leaving unnecessary extra terms.

solutions.fullSolution:
phi_1 = x_1 + x_-1 - 2*x_0 = x_1 (boundary terms are zero). phi_2 = x_2 + x_0 - 2*x_1 = x_2 - 2*x_1. phi_3 = x_2 - 5.
J = [[d phi_1/dx_1, d phi_1/dx_2], [d phi_2/dx_1, d phi_2/dx_2], [d phi_3/dx_1, d phi_3/dx_2]] = [[1,0],[-2,1],[0,1]].
The zero entries (phi_1 not depending on x_2, phi_3 not depending on x_1) reflect that each term in the path-optimization cost only involves a small, local window of consecutive timesteps. In a path with many timesteps, this locality means J is banded/sparse (each row has only 2-3 nonzero entries regardless of path length), which is exactly what keeps J^T J sparse and Gauss-Newton tractable for long trajectories.

criteria.description: Correctly counts 3 free parameters for a symmetric 2x2 matrix vs 2 scalar equations from the secant equation.
Correctly connects this underdetermination to why BFGS needs a specific update rule.

solutions.fullSolution:
H-hat*delta = [[2,1],[1,3]]@[1,0] = [2,1] = y. Yes, it satisfies the secant equation.
A symmetric 2x2 matrix has 3 free parameters (2 diagonal entries + 1 off-diagonal, since the matrix is symmetric). The secant equation H-hat*delta=y is a vector equation with 2 scalar components. So 3 unknowns, 2 equations: underdetermined, a whole 1-parameter family of symmetric matrices satisfies this single secant equation exactly. This is why BFGS doesn't just 'solve' the secant equation: it specifies a particular rank-2 update rule that picks out one specific matrix from that family, one that also incorporates and smoothly updates the PREVIOUS estimate's information, rather than being arbitrary.

A*delta1 = diag(1,4)@[-1.545,0.097] = [-1.545, 0.388]. delta0^T(A*delta1) = (-2)*(-1.545) + (-8)*(0.388) = 3.09 - 3.104 = approx -0.01, i.e. approximately zero (the tiny residual is rounding in the given delta1; exactly zero algebraically). This confirms delta0 and delta1 are H-conjugate, i.e. delta1 doesn't interfere with progress already made along delta0 under the metric induced by A, exactly the property CG's Polak-Ribiere construction guarantees for a quadratic objective. (Independently verified by running the full CG algorithm in NumPy while authoring this module: conjugacy held to floating-point precision, ~1e-16.)
